note: Meiklejohn's translation prints no A/B pages. By the owner's choice (2026-11-21, “Scholars' citations plus Akademie page”), each number comes from Kemp Smith's Commentary or a current SEP entry that quotes or cites the same sentence, matched to Meiklejohn by content, and the German sentence's Akademie page was checked by script; the table is under ab. Passages with no such source are quoted without a page (listed under unread). Kant is public domain, so he is quoted exactly from the bundled book, each quotation under 15 words: the full text is one tap away, and each page reference opens its passage. Interpretation is credited to named scholarship only. Kemp Smith (1918) is the oldest scholarship used; it is cited for page numbers, the A/B edition differences and his reading of the noumenon revision, which is given as his.
disputes: transcendental-idealism, noumenon: one object or two? Rohlf (SEP, 2024): “there is no such thing as the standard interpretation of Kant's transcendental idealism”; he sets out a two-objects reading (from the Garve–Feder review) and a two-aspects reading (Langton 1998, property dualism; Allison 2004, two standpoints). Stang (SEP, 2016) treats phenomenalist, epistemic (Prauss, Allison, Bird) and metaphysical dual-aspect readings (Langton), and lists one-object and two-object readers in §5. Recorded open; the entries report the readings and settle none.

noumenon: what the second edition's revision of the phenomena and noumena chapter does. Kemp Smith reads it as making the existence of things in themselves “quite explicit”; this is his reading, given as his. Stang §6, which treats the chapter, was not read (see unread).

new_d.text: Kant's doctrine that space and time are forms of our sensible intuition, so that we cognize things only as they appear to us and never as they are in themselves.

new_text.text: The second preface proposes an experiment modelled on Copernicus: metaphysics should try assuming “that the objects must conform to our cognition” (Bxvi).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 33

new_text.text: On that assumption a priori cognition becomes possible, since “we only cognize in things a priori that which we ourselves place in them” (Bxviii).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 33

new_text.text: Kant still reserves the power of thinking things in themselves, since otherwise we would affirm “an appearance, without something that appears” (Bxxvi–xxvii).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 41

new_text.text: Limiting speculative reason in this way serves the practical: “I must, therefore, abolish knowledge, to make room for belief” (Bxxx).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 43

new_text.text: The Transcendental Aesthetic argues the doctrine for space and time.

claims.by: CPR A19–49/B33–73 (framing; the sentences that follow carry their pages)

new_text.text: “Space does not represent any property of objects as things in themselves” (A26/B42).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 119

new_text.text: Kant therefore maintains “the empirical reality of space” for all possible outer experience, together with its transcendental ideality (A28/B44).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 121

new_text.text: What we call outward objects are “nothing else but mere representations of our sensibility” (A30/B45), whose real correlate, the thing in itself, these representations never make known.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 122

new_text.text: The things we intuit “are not in themselves the same as our representations of them in intuition” (A42/B59).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 145

new_text.text: The name comes in the chapter on the antinomy.
Everything intuited in space and time is phenomenon, mere representation, with no self-subsistent existence apart from human thought: “This doctrine I call Transcendental Idealism” (A491/B519).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 869

new_text.text: A note adds that Kant has elsewhere called it “formal idealism”, to distinguish it from material idealism, which doubts or denies the existence of external things (A491/B519).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 870

new_text.text: The antinomy also yields an indirect proof (A506/B534).
If the world were a whole existing in itself it would be finite or infinite; it is neither, so phenomena “are nothing, apart from our representations”.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 887

new_text.text: Two features of this translation matter here.

Meiklejohn renders Kant's Erscheinung (appearance) as “phenomenon” almost throughout, as Norman Kemp Smith points out in his Commentary (1918), so his “phenomena” usually stand for what Kant calls appearances.
new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 6, 29

new_text.text: And it translates the second edition, which drops the Fourth Paralogism, where the first edition defines transcendental idealism as “the doctrine that they are all together to be regarded as mere representations”, in the Guyer and Wood translation Nicholas Stang quotes from A369.
new_text.quotes: 1 from the scholarship, verbatim in its literal text

new_text.text: Michael Rohlf's Stanford Encyclopedia entry (revised 2024) states that “there is no such thing as the standard interpretation of Kant's transcendental idealism”.
new_text.quotes: 1 from the scholarship, verbatim in its literal text

new_text.text: He sets out a two-objects reading, which counts appearances and things in themselves as two classes of objects and goes back to the Göttingen review by Christian Garve and J. G. Feder, and a two-aspects reading of one world, in a property-dualist version (Rae Langton, 1998) and an epistemological version of two standpoints (Henry Allison, 2004).
Stang credits the epistemic reading to Gerold Prauss, Allison and Graham Bird, and calls Langton's “Perhaps the most influential metaphysical but non-phenomenalist interpretation”.
new_text.quotes: 1 from the scholarship, verbatim in its literal text

new_text.text: Whether appearances and things in themselves are one object or two stays disputed (see Phenomenon and noumenon).

old.text: Nicholas Stang sums up the doctrine: space and time are “the forms of our sensible intuition of objects”, and “We cannot cognize things in themselves”, though we can think about them using the categories.
old.note: cut; the second preface (Bxix–xx, Bxxvi–xxvii) now states the doctrine in Kant's words

old.text: Kant calls the thing in itself “something actual for itself but uncognized by us”, and interpreters divide between a two-objects and a two-aspects reading of the distinction.
old.note: replaced by Meiklejohn's own wording (B308, A255/B310–11) and Kemp Smith's reading of the revision; the two-readings point moved to transcendental-idealism, where Rohlf and Stang set it out

old.text: Jacobi, and Fichte after him, objected that Kant's account of affection is inconsistent: the objects that affect our senses can be neither things in themselves, since that would apply the categories to them, nor appearances, which depend on the very experiences they would cause; Jacobi wrote that “without the presupposition of the [thing in itself] I cannot enter the [critical] system”.
Paul Redding reports that post-Kantian interpreters see Hegel as furthering Kant's critique “into the very coherence of a conception of an in-itself reality”.
Nick Land's collected writings of 1987–2007 are titled Fanged Noumena.

new_d.text: Kant: phenomena are things as they appear to us, under the forms of space and time and the categories. The noumenon, or thing in itself, is a thing considered apart from our way of intuiting it, which we can think but cannot cognize.

new_text.text: The second preface states the result.
Our a priori cognition “has only to do with phenomena”, and things in themselves, “while possessing a real existence, lie beyond its sphere” (Bxix–xx).
new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 35, 35

new_text.text: We keep the power of thinking them, since otherwise there would be “an appearance, without something that appears” (Bxxvi–xxvii).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 41

new_text.text: The chapter on phenomena and noumena distinguishes two senses.

claims.by: CPR B306–7, block 528 (no A/B source found; quoted without a page)

new_text.text: A thing so far as it is not an object of our sensuous intuition is a noumenon “in the negative sense of the word”; the object of an intellectual intuition, a mode of intuition which does not belong to us, would be a noumenon “in the positive sense”.

claims.by: CPR B307, block 528 (no A/B source found; quoted without a page)

new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 528, 528

new_text.text: Without the unity of intuitions in space and time, “the whole meaning of the categories is entirely lost” (B308), so what we call noumenon “must be understood by us as such in a negative sense”.
new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 529, 529

new_text.text: The concept is not self-contradictory, and it is needed “to restrain sensuous intuition within the bounds of phenomena” (A255/B310–11); it is “merely a limitative conception and therefore only of negative use” (A255/B310–11).
new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 531, 531

new_text.text: The division of objects into phenomena and noumena is “quite inadmissible in a positive sense” (A255/B311).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 532

new_text.text: Kant revised this chapter for the second edition, and first-edition paragraphs of it, among them parts of A 241–2 and A 248–53, are absent from Meiklejohn's translation.

new_text.text: Norman Kemp Smith's Commentary (1918) reads the revision as a hardening.

Where the first edition called the division of objects into phenomena and noumena “not in any way admissible”, the second adds the words “in the positive sense”, and in Kemp Smith's reading “the assumption that things in themselves actually exist becomes quite explicit”.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 528; 2 from the scholarship, verbatim in its literal text

new_text.text: Whether appearances and things in themselves are one object or two, interpreters still dispute (see Transcendental idealism).

Jacobi, and Fichte after him, objected that Kant's account of affection is inconsistent: the objects that affect our senses can be neither things in themselves, since that would apply the categories to them, nor appearances, which depend on the very experiences they would cause; Jacobi wrote that “without the presupposition of the [thing in itself] I cannot enter the [critical] system”.

old.text: Georges Rey writes that the possibility of the synthetic a priori “became a major concern” of Kant's work, and that Kant argued that “even so elementary an example in arithmetic as 7+5=12 is synthetic”; his concern extended to geometry as well.
Kant treats the law that every event has a cause as one that the sensible world conforms to and that can be known a priori.
old.note: replaced by Kant's own example read in Meiklejohn (A9/B13)

old.text: His answer is that sensibility contributes space and time as a priori forms of intuition and the understanding contributes the categories, so that “we can cognize of things a priori only what we ourselves have put into them”.
old.note: replaced by Bxviii in Meiklejohn's words (the old quotation was Rohlf's Guyer–Wood rendering)

old.text: In the nineteenth century Gauss, Riemann and Lobachevsky developed non-Euclidean geometries as conceptual possibilities, and in 1916 Einstein argued that physics seemed to favour one of them over Euclid's.
The logical positivists hoped logical analysis would show that the rest of our knowledge, beyond mathematics, rests on logic and experience combined.

new_d.text: Kant's claim that some judgments add content to their concepts and are still known independently of experience.

new_text.text: Kant divides judgments by how the predicate stands to the subject.

Either “the predicate B belongs to the subject A” as something contained, though covertly, in its concept, or it lies outside the concept while connected with it; the first judgment he calls analytical, the second synthetical (A6/B10).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 70

new_text.text: “Judgements of experience, as such, are always synthetical” (B11), since an analytical judgment needs no appeal to experience.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 71

new_text.text: Synthetical judgments a priori raise the difficulty.

In “Everything that happens has a cause” (A9/B13), the concept of cause lies outside the concept of something that happens, and the proposition claims a universality and necessity which experience cannot give (A9/B13).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 72

new_text.text: Mathematics holds such judgments too: we might take 7 + 5 = 12 for analytical, but the concept of the sum of seven and five “contains nothing more than the uniting of both sums into one” (B15).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 76

new_text.text: The task of the whole work comes under one question: “How are synthetical judgements a priori possible?” (B19).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 81

new_text.text: The answer begins from the experiment of the second preface: “we only cognize in things a priori that which we ourselves place in them” (Bxviii).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 33

new_text.text: Space and time, as forms of intuition, and the categories of the understanding supply what such a judgment adds (see Transcendental idealism; Categories of the understanding).

synthetic-a-priori.s: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (1781; 2nd ed. 1787), Bxviii, A6–10/B10–19; Prolegomena (1783), §5

new_d.text: Kant's twelve pure concepts of the understanding, which he derives from the logical forms of judgment and argues hold a priori of every object of possible experience.

new_text.text: Cognition needs two faculties: sensibility, through which objects are given, and understanding, through which they are thought.
“Thoughts without content are void; intuitions without conceptions, blind” (A51/B75).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 163

new_text.text: The function that unites representations in a judgment “gives also unity to the mere synthesis of different representations in an intuition”, and “this unity we call the pure conception of the understanding” (A79/B105).
new_text.quotes: 2 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 212, 212

new_text.text: There are therefore as many pure conceptions as there are logical functions of judgment, and Kant, “with Aristotle”, calls them categories, while noting the great difference in execution.

claims.by: CPR A79–80/B105, block 213 (follows A79/B105; no separate A/B source, quoted without a page)

new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 213

new_text.text: His Table of the Categories (A80/B106) has four heads of three: quantity (unity, plurality, totality), quality (reality, negation, limitation), relation (inherence and subsistence, causality and dependence, community) and modality (possibility and impossibility, existence and non-existence, necessity and contingence).

Kant calls this derivation from the forms of judgment the metaphysical deduction; in Michael Rohlf's examples, the categorical form of judgment yields substance and accident, and the hypothetical form, cause and effect.
The transcendental deduction asks by what right these concepts apply to objects.
The second edition's version starts from self-consciousness: the I think, Kant writes, must “accompany all my representations” (B131).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 256

new_text.text: Rohlf reads the deduction as showing that the categories are objectively valid because they are necessary conditions of experience.

The first edition's version of the deduction, A 95–130, with its threefold synthesis and the passage at A 125–6 where the understanding is the legislation for nature, is absent from Meiklejohn's translation.

claims.by: CPR, German A and B texts compared; KS for A 95–130; KNT quotes A125–126

new_text.text: The categories have no use beyond possible experience: for noumena, “the whole meaning of the categories is entirely lost” (B308).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 529

new_d.text: Kant's name for the conflict reason falls into when it thinks the world as a completed whole: four pairs of opposed propositions, thesis and antithesis, each of which seems provable.

new_text.text: Seeking the unconditioned for every conditioned, reason meets “a perfectly natural antithetic”, into which it falls of itself.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 712

new_text.text: It is tempted either to a despairing scepticism or to dogmatic obstinacy, and the scepticism “might perhaps deserve the title of the euthanasia of pure reason” (A407/B434).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 712

new_text.text: The Antithetic (A420/B448) sets out four conflicts.
In the first, the world “has a beginning in time, and is also limited in regard to space”, against a world infinite in time and space.

claims.by: CPR first conflict, blocks 745, 751 (no A/B source for the statements)

new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 745

new_text.text: In the second, every composite substance consists of simple parts, against there being no simple substance in the world.

claims.by: CPR second conflict, blocks 769, 774 (no A/B source for the statements; KS gives A420/B448 for the section)

new_text.text: In the third, a causality of freedom is needed besides causality by the laws of nature, against “There is no such thing as freedom”.

claims.by: CPR third conflict, blocks 787, 792 (no A/B source for the statements)

new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 792

new_text.text: In the fourth, an absolutely necessary being exists, in the world or as its cause, against there being none.

claims.by: CPR fourth conflict, blocks 805, 810 (no A/B source for the statements)

new_text.text: Michelle Grier notes that both sides argue apagogically, establishing their conclusions by indirect proof.
Behind the conflict stands one argument: if the conditioned is given, “the whole series of its conditions is also given” (A497/B525), and sensuous objects are given as conditioned.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 877

new_text.text: Grier reports Kant's diagnosis of this syllogism as an ambiguous middle term, which takes the conditioned as a pure concept in the major premise and empirically in the minor.
Kant's diagnosis is that the idea of absolute totality is “admissible only as a condition of things in themselves” (A506/B534), and applied to phenomena it produces an illusory opposition.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 887

new_text.text: The same passage draws from the antinomy an indirect proof of transcendental idealism.
The first two antinomies, the mathematical ones, are ended “by declaring both contradictory statements to be false” (A528/B556).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 922

new_text.text: In the two dynamical ones a condition outside the series of phenomena is admissible, so “both propositions of reason may be shown to be true in their proper signification”.
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 925

new_text.text: The solution of the third begins from two modes of causality, “the causality of nature or of freedom” (A532/B560).
new_text.quotes: 1 of Kant's (Meiklejohn) verbatim in the bundled book, blocks 928

new_text.text: Grier notes that Kant claims the resolution provides “an indirect argument for his own transcendental idealism”, and she lists detailed discussions of the antinomies by Al-Azm, Bennett, Guyer, Strawson, Watkins, Van Cleve and others.
new_text.quotes: 1 from the scholarship, verbatim in its literal text

summary: Three new entries (transcendental idealism, categories of the understanding, antinomy of pure reason) and two re-reads (phenomenon and noumenon, synthetic a priori), read in the bundled Meiklejohn Critique first and the Stanford Encyclopedia second (Rohlf 2024, Stang 2016, Grier 2022, Rey 2026), with Kemp Smith's Commentary (1918) for A/B pages and the first-edition differences. 28 A/B references, each matched by content to a scholar's citation and checked against the Akademie page; each opens its passage in the book. Two disputes recorded: one object or two (open), and Kemp Smith's reading of the second-edition revision of the noumenon chapter (given as his; Stang §6 unread).
